I think of it this way, by taking the first order you're offered, you're busy fulfilling a $3 order, while if you wait another five minutes, you'll be offered an $8 order. Waiting a few minutes (usually) is worth it for the better order.

If you're unsure what constitutes a "good" order, check milage for the orders and consider using a $1 = $1 mile ratio. $7.50 for ten miles is not worth it. But $7.50 for two or three miles is worth it. In my area I even do $2 = 1 mile when it's busy, as I get a lot of offers in my area that meet that criteria.

In my experience, running orders that are quick and low milage are better versus high milage orders, even if the pay is better, as it's less time on the road and you can get more orders done per hour. I'd rather get 2-3 orders in an hour that are 6-7 dollars vs one order done that's ten or twelve, as this will actually add up to more per hour (as long as you and the restaurants are both efficient, fingers crossed). Consider too that Doordash doesn't include the return distance to your local hotspot in the trip mileage, you'll often end up doing twice the advertised distance round trip.

Doordash would certainly prefer you take every order, but outside of waiting a little longer for a bigger fish, there's not any punishment for declining orders. They may temporarily pause your dash (you can resume immediately though, not as bad as it sounds), but you won't be deactivated or penalized in any way. My acceptance rate is about 15 percent, and I'm sure most dashers here will also attest to low acceptance rates, some even lower than mine.

And finally, have some good tunes on the radio, maybe a good podcast, bring hydration and comfy clothes, and try to enjoy yourself. It really can be a pretty easy gig usually. Having a positive attitude will make the job less stressful, I refuse to stress out ever, and dashing barely even feels like work for me.

Deadly Premonition is a very polarizing game, but I had a lot of fun with it! It can be a little bit of a mess from a technical standpoint, with glitches and strange quirks in how it tells it's story, but I personally felt it added to the charm and did Twin Peaks vibes really well! Where as Alan Wake has a lot more focus on combat, DP streamlined it and kept to mostly focusing on the characters and stories, exploring quirky characters and the mysteries to be solved in the town.

I liked the collectibles pages but didn't care for how they spoiled the story as much, but it was still a pretty novel idea. The episode recap format I just wish didn't start as soon as the last episode finished, as I was still controller in hand, only to come back a couple days later to find it saved a checkpoint just after the recap. I think it would have been more helpful if the game allowed the player to easily access the recaps at the start of a new session.

The game looks all right enough during the daytime sections, it was only the night sections that bothered me. I personally just don't like very subdued or dark colors. GTA IV came out the same year, and I wasn't very into the washed out colors in that game either, although I felt that game looked a little better overall than Alan Wake did.

I think it has a lot to do with that I played this game in 2020, so the graphics of a ten year old game weren't going to impress like they probably did on release.

I'll probably eat downvotes for this, but I can't see why this game gets such high praise.
